title: Bias, stereotypes, misconceptions and loaded language
blurb: Spot one-sided writing from its fingerprints: loaded words, missing evidence, cherry-picked data, stereotypes and hidden interests.
question: A blog post praising a clinic's late-night hours calls its critics “grumbling bureaucrats,” cites one survey of night visitors, and never mentions that the author owns the staffing company. What signs of bias are in the post, and how do you name them on the TEAS?

teach.body: Formally, bias is a one-sided presentation that favors a particular viewpoint. A biased text may be accurate sentence by sentence and still mislead, because of what it emphasizes, leaves out or how it words things. Plain English: a biased writer has a thumb on the scale. Your TEAS job is to find the thumb, name it, and keep it separate from two related ideas: stereotypes and misconceptions.

children.label: Undisclosed interest
children.sub: a maker funds its own study

teach.caption: Ask three questions: How is it worded? What was chosen or left out? Who benefits?
A passage that corrects a misconception is not biased for doing so: it is replacing a wrong belief with evidence.

head: Loaded
Neutral
Slant
teach.caption: Loaded language uses connotation (the feeling a word carries) to push the reader without adding evidence.

teach.h: Scenario: Darnell reads a blog post
teach.body: Darnell, a nursing applicant, reads this post: “Critics of the downtown clinic's late-night hours are a few grumbling bureaucrats who have never worked a night shift. The truth is simple: patients love the change. A survey of night visitors found that 9 in 10 were satisfied. Young people, who are always out late anyway, are the main users. Anyone who wants to slash these hours is gambling with lives.” A note at the bottom says the author's company staffs the night shift.

items: “Grumbling bureaucrats”: attacks the critics as people, not their reasons. That is ad hominem.
“Slash” and “gambling with lives”: emotional, loaded words in place of evidence.
The survey asked night visitors only, the group most likely to approve. That is cherry-picked data.
“Young people, who are always out late anyway”: an oversimplified label for a whole group. That is a stereotype.
No costs, staffing problems or critics' actual reasons appear: omitted counterevidence.
The author profits from the night shift and does not say so in the argument: an undisclosed interest.

teach.body: A misconception is a commonly held but incorrect belief. Writers often set one up in order to correct it: “Many people think cold weather causes colds, but...” The signal is a common belief followed by a contrast word and evidence. The author does not hold the misconception; they are knocking it down. The same goes for views an author reports and refutes: quoting an opponent is not the same as agreeing with them.

teach.caption: If a TEAS option says the author “believes” the first box, it has mixed up the author's view with the view being refuted.

teach.text: Classic traps: calling an author biased because they quote a view they then refute; calling a passage neutral because it contains statistics, when the statistics were cherry-picked; and calling a single loaded word a “stereotype.” A stereotype is about a GROUP of people. Loaded language is about word choice.

items: Bias: a one-sided presentation that favors a viewpoint.
Bias signs: loaded language, ad hominem, omitted counterevidence, cherry-picked data, unequal treatment, undisclosed interests.
Stereotype: an oversimplified generalization about a group.
Misconception: a common but incorrect belief, often set up so the author can correct it.
Quoting or reporting a view is not the same as holding it.

summary: You can now name the signs of bias (loaded language, ad hominem, omitted counterevidence, cherry-picked data, unequal treatment and undisclosed interests). You can also tell a stereotype from a misconception, and an author's own view from one they report and refute.

A.q: Which sentence from a community forum relies on a stereotype?
options: Some patients over 70 asked for help with the portal.
The patient portal crashed twice during the update.
Older patients just can't handle online portals.
The portal's menu is cluttered and hard to follow.
A.why: It makes an oversimplified generalization about an entire group (older patients). That is a stereotype.

whyNot.0: This describes what some specific patients did; it does not label the whole group.
whyNot.1: This is a checkable fact about the portal, not a claim about a group of people.
whyNot.3: This is an opinion about the portal's design, but it says nothing about a group of people.

A.q: “The hospital's bureaucrats implemented a new parking fee of $5 a day for visitors.” Which word is loaded language?
options: hospital's
bureaucrats
implemented
visitors
A.why: “Bureaucrats” carries a negative connotation of rigid, rule-bound officials. The neutral word would be “administrators.”

whyNot.0: “Hospital's” names the institution involved; it carries no slant.
whyNot.2: “Implemented” states what happened without judging it.
whyNot.3: “Visitors” neutrally names the people who will pay the fee.

A.q: “Many people think reading in dim light permanently damages the eyes. Eye doctors report that it can cause temporary eyestrain but no lasting harm.” What is the author doing in the first sentence?
options: Stating a misconception the passage then corrects
Revealing a bias against the eye doctors' findings
Presenting a stereotype about people who read a lot
Offering the author's own view about reading in dim light
A.why: The author sets up a commonly held but incorrect belief and then corrects it with what eye doctors report. That is the misconception pattern.

whyNot.1: The author agrees with the eye doctors; the passage is built to support their view.
whyNot.2: A stereotype labels a group of people; this sentence is about a belief, not a group's traits.
whyNot.3: The author reports what “many people think” in order to refute it, so it is not the author's view.

B.q: A website article titled “Why Vita-Boost Beats Every Other Vitamin” cites a study showing the product improves energy. The article does not mention that Vita-Boost's maker paid for the study. Which form of bias does this illustrate?
options: An ad hominem attack on rival brands
A stereotype about people who take vitamins
A misconception the article corrects
An undisclosed interest behind the evidence
B.why: The company that profits from the product funded the study, and the article hides that. An undisclosed interest is a classic sign of bias.

whyNot.0: The article does not attack any person or rival; it promotes its own product.
whyNot.1: Nothing labels a whole group of people.
whyNot.2: The article does not set up and correct a common false belief.

B.q: A school district newsletter announces, “Third graders at Oak Hill Elementary raised their reading scores 22 points with our new program!” It does not mention that scores fell at the district's four other elementary schools. Which best describes the bias?
options: Cherry-picked data that favors the program
A stereotype about third-grade readers as a group
Loaded language that attacks the program's critics
An expert opinion presented as a fact
B.why: The newsletter reports the one result that flatters the program and leaves out the four that do not. That is cherry-picking.

whyNot.1: No oversimplified label is applied to third graders as a group.
whyNot.2: The newsletter does not mention or attack critics at all.
whyNot.3: No expert is quoted; the issue is which data were selected.

B.q: “Some residents claim the new library branch is a waste of tax money, a luxury in the age of smartphones. Yet the branch logged 48,000 visits in its first year, and its free job-search workshops are booked weeks in advance.” A student says the author thinks the branch is a luxury. Why is the student mistaken?
options: The author presents both sides with equal support
The author reports the claim in order to refute it
The author agrees the branch costs too much money
The author relies on loaded words to attack residents
B.why: The “luxury” view belongs to “some residents.” The author answers it with “Yet” and evidence of heavy use, so the author's own view is favorable.

whyNot.0: Only the library's side gets evidence; the critics' claim is stated and then answered.
whyNot.2: The passage argues the opposite: the visits and full workshops show the branch is valued.
whyNot.3: The author does not name-call the residents; the passage answers them with data.

C.q: “The so-called health experts pushing the soda tax are out-of-touch elites who sip imported water and lecture working families. The tax would add two cents per ounce. Corner stores in Fresno, one owner told me, could lose customers.” Which best describes how the author's bias is shown in the first sentence?
options: It cites the tax rate without explaining its effect
It relies on a single store owner's secondhand account
It attacks supporters rather than their reasons
It corrects a common belief about soda taxes
C.why: Calling supporters “out-of-touch elites who sip imported water” attacks their character, not their argument. That is ad hominem, a sign of bias.

whyNot.0: The tax rate appears in the second sentence, and stating it is factual, not biased.
whyNot.1: Relying on one owner is weak evidence, but it is in the third sentence, not the first.
whyNot.3: The first sentence does not set up and correct a misconception; it insults a group.

C.q: An article argues that a hospital should switch all nurses to 12-hour shifts. It quotes three nurses who prefer longer shifts and describes the money the hospital would save. Which additional information would make the article more balanced?
options: A fourth nurse who prefers working 12-hour shifts
Concerns raised by staff who oppose the change
The exact yearly savings in dollars for the hospital
Praise for the plan from the chief executive
C.why: The article omits counterevidence. Including the reasons of staff who oppose the switch would treat both sides more equally.

whyNot.0: Another supporter adds to the same side, which makes the slant stronger, not weaker.
whyNot.2: More precise savings figures add more support to the side the article already favors.
whyNot.3: Praise from the chief executive adds another voice on the side the article already favors, so the slant grows.

C.q: “The mayor's lackeys rammed the budget through in a single night.” Which revision removes the loaded language while keeping the same facts?
options: The mayor's lackeys passed the budget in one evening.
The mayor's allies rammed the budget through in one evening.
The mayor's allies passed the budget in one evening.
The mayor's allies passed a budget most residents oppose.
C.why: “Allies” replaces the negative “lackeys,” and “passed” replaces the forceful “rammed through,” while the facts (who, what, when) stay the same.

whyNot.0: “Lackeys” is still there, so the loaded language remains.
whyNot.1: “Rammed through” is still there, so the loaded language remains.
whyNot.3: This adds a new claim about residents' views that was not in the original sentence.

reteach.title: The rigged highlight reel
reteach.question: A sports channel shows only one team's goals and calls the other team's players “clumsy.” Is the reel lying, or just slanted? Bias in writing works the same way.

blocks.h: Every clip is real, the reel is not fair
blocks.body: Each goal in the reel really happened, yet viewers come away with a false picture because the other team's goals were cut (omitted counterevidence), the best clips were chosen (cherry-picking), the commentator mocks opposing players (ad hominem) and uses words like “sloppy” (loaded language). If the channel is owned by one team, that is an undisclosed interest. A writer can be accurate sentence by sentence and still be biased in exactly these ways.

blocks.text: A stereotype is different: it is the commentator saying “all players from that city are lazy.” It labels a whole group, not one opponent, and that is what separates it from an ad hominem attack.

explain.body: Bias is a one-sided presentation. Look for loaded or emotional words, attacks on people (ad hominem), missing counterevidence, cherry-picked data, one side getting more space or kinder treatment, and interests the writer does not disclose.

test.q: A review of a new blood-pressure monitor quotes four happy customers, does not mention a recall notice issued for the device last month, and is posted on the manufacturer's website. Which sign of bias is NOT present in this review?
options: Omitted counterevidence
Selective, one-sided sources
A source that benefits from sales
An attack on rival companies
test.why: Nothing in the review attacks a rival or a critic as a person, so there is no ad hominem attack. The other three signs are all present.

whyNot.0: The recall notice is left out, which is omitted counterevidence.
whyNot.1: Quoting only happy customers is a one-sided selection of sources.
whyNot.2: The manufacturer profits from sales and is the one publishing the review.

explain.body: Loaded words carry strong positive or negative connotations that push the reader's feelings without adding evidence: “regime” instead of “government,” “scheme” instead of “plan,” “slash” instead of “reduce.” To test a word, swap in a neutral synonym and see whether the facts change. If they do not, the original word was doing emotional work.

test.q: A news report says a union “staged a stunt” outside City Hall. Which phrase would report the same event in neutral language?
options: held a rally
threw a tantrum
made a scene
led a heroic stand
test.why: “Held a rally” describes the event without praising or mocking it.

whyNot.1: “Threw a tantrum” is even more negative than the original; it mocks the union.
whyNot.2: “Made a scene” still carries a negative, disapproving slant.
whyNot.3: “Heroic stand” swaps a negative slant for a positive one; it is still loaded.

explain.body: A stereotype is an oversimplified generalization about a group of people: “All teenagers are reckless.” It ignores individual differences. A claim about a group backed by specific data (“In the survey, 40% of the teen drivers...”) is not a stereotype, because it reports evidence rather than labeling everyone.

test.q: Which sentence from a parenting magazine contains a stereotype?
options: In our poll, 58% of fathers said they cook dinner weekly.
Dads, of course, are hopeless in the kitchen.
Many of the fathers we polled worked night shifts.
The poll included 300 fathers from 12 states.
test.why: It labels all fathers as hopeless cooks, an oversimplified generalization about a group.

whyNot.0: This reports a poll result about a specific sample, not a label for all fathers.
whyNot.2: This describes the polled fathers specifically, which can be checked.
whyNot.3: This describes the poll's sample size and spread, a checkable fact.

explain.body: A misconception is a common but incorrect belief. Authors often introduce one (“Many people assume...”) to correct it with evidence. Neither the misconception nor a quoted opponent's view is the author's own. Read past the contrast word (but, however, in fact) to find what the author actually thinks.

test.q: “Contrary to popular belief, sugar does not make most children hyperactive. Controlled studies in which neither parents nor children knew who received sugar found no difference in behavior.” What is the purpose of the phrase “Contrary to popular belief”?
options: To reveal the author's bias in favor of sugar makers
To label parents with an unfair stereotype
To show that the author shares the popular belief
To signal that a misconception will be corrected
test.why: The phrase sets up a widely held belief so that the author can correct it with study evidence.

whyNot.0: Nothing in the passage links the author to sugar makers; the claim rests on controlled studies.
whyNot.1: No oversimplified label is applied to parents as a group.
whyNot.2: The author rejects the popular belief; the phrase introduces it in order to refute it.
